As described here, I am looking for ideas/suggestions on how to deal with users abusing voat and submitting links to a single website, targeting a single sub and doing so several times per day. Banning users is not the way to go because creating a new account takes <1 minute.

My proposal was to allow website.com to be submitted only a certain number of times to sub x in a 24 hour period.

Thoughts? Ideas? Please leave a comment here or on GitHub.

Upon reading the first part of your inquiry, the very first thing I thought to was, "Only permit X number of submissions for a domain daily."

You could certainly do that... though my thought would be to write an algorithm that would apply a weight to a domain... For example, someone linking to cnn.com articles would not necessarily hit threshold because it's a well know, established site that we "know." (I have no affiliation with cnn.com nor do I even go there, just using that site for example... I could have used sun.com or weather.com...)

The specifics of the algorithm would need to be tailored for the submissions you're experiencing, but the general idea would definitely work. "bobspicklebarrel.com" isn't as well known as "cnn.com" and therefore would have less allowed submissions per day. If cnn.com were allowed 50, bob...'s would be allowed... 5. For sake of example and easy numbers.

Now, as bob...'s website is linked to by legitimate accounts (think accounts that are active and operating, not just submitting links to the same site, etc.) it's "cred" goes up and it eventually permits higher volumes of submissions... I suggest the user check because that is what's going to protect you from the new user spam... You simply make the new users submitting the site useless: They add no cred to the domain, in fact you could make those accounts reduce the domain's cred.

Of course, you could scratch that (A lot of domains and all, right? Who wants to do that work?) and just set up some checks and balances that checks for so many submissions so quickly for the domain and do a graylist of the domain for a period of time. The graylist would consist of the domain and the timestamp for it to be "removed" from the list (it shouldn't actually be removed, just do this via timestamp because if it's a spamming domain, it's going to be on the list again).

Now... ALL of that said: ANY of these mechanics can be bypassed in some manner or exploited to negatively impact a competitor (for sake of example). Just be careful with the methodology... because you have source out there, and anybody with a little knowledge, some time, and an intent could break your systems and spam all they want. The key is to make the punishment of doing all of that work outweigh the benefit.

Take care, Atko. As always, you know how to reach me via PM.

I remembered on "that other site", the Admins could see the IP address of people.

Those who spam or create pure havoc would have their IP address banned. This solves the problem of spammers creating a new account, because even if they did that IP is toast.

But once again, a lot of trust would have to be given to the admins not to abuse this.

Spam bots don't get affected by this as they can easily change their IP address. So can you, in like two minutes.

Also, for the record, this very reason is why shadowbanning was created.

I think the ip tracking would be most helpful if possible, although you can obviously mask that if you're determined. As others pointed out, sites like bbc or Reuters, youtube, imgur etc. are more credible and have more valid content, so one size fits all content limits would somewhat break things. Giving sites more links available by algorithm might actually require a lot of micromanagement if things need tweaking or other abuses occur.

It's tough nut to crack. I.P. Management and mod management plus a mechanism to remove mods abusing power should keep things clean. Additionally spam could result in a subverse ban for a period or a site wide ban for a period, depending on severity. I think you have to let them cheat, and punish, not pre-emptively put barriers in place.

Require any further submissions past a certain threshold to link to website archives. I'm sure that this problem won't be as problematic if voat grows and more people downvote this spam.

Or you could place a mandatory flair on their accounts that vilifies them as spammers or affiliated to that site (if that's known).

I would suggest something like Reddit's shadow banning for spammers, which is quite effective at controlling them.

The problem is that it's far too open for abuse to silence discussion or censor stuff you don't want. A very strict and completely transparent usage policy would be needed including repercussions for admins who abuse it.

An easy way to quell this is to write the script to actually post to a sub listing why the user was banned and the evidence used to ban them. That is automation including complete transparency. Of course, you'd have to code both the automated algorithm in addition to the manual interface for those individuals who are manually handled (such as abusers, harassers, etc.). The payloads would be the same for both processes: ban the username and IP, post to a locked down sub that only the system can write to listing the reason for ban (can be a populated dropdown for the admin to choose a reason), and a list of comments/messages/text that supports why the ban took place.

I think primarily a post/time limit needs to be set, barring links to whitelisted sites. IMO this should include posting the same link to multiple subs as well. If this site's staff can tolerate some interaction on this topic, there could be a warning that is issued via PM to users whose submissions to shitsite.com are over some percentage over time asking why their posting privileges shouldn't be throttled or revoked. This avoids the obnoxious shadowban issue and gives abusive users the opportunity to clean up their act. It also avoids stomping on users who are innocently posting to the same site in a sub that is created for that purpose (like say, /v/xkcd).
